examples.label: a*b*  (right-linear)
examples.purpose: Right-linear grammar: each step extends the word on the right.
text: S -> a S | b B | eps

examples.label: (ab)+  (left-linear)
examples.purpose: Left-linear grammar: the word grows to the left of the nonterminal.
text: // Rules: A -> B w  (nonterminal on the left of the terminal)
// Compare with the right-linear version: S -> a B, B -> b S | b
S -> S a b | a b

examples.label: Even number of a's  (left-linear)
examples.purpose: Counting as a grammar: the nonterminals record the parity.
text: // Left-linear grammar for strings over {a,b} with an even number of a's
// S = even count so far (accepting);  A = odd count so far
// Rules: A -> B w  (nonterminal then terminal)
S -> A a | S b | eps

examples.label: Strings ending in ab  (right-linear)
examples.purpose: Suffix language: the nonterminals track progress towards the final ab.
text: S -> a S | b S | a A

examples.label: Balanced a…b  (aⁿbⁿ)
examples.purpose: Standard non-regular context-free language: matching pairs built from the outside in.

examples.label: Palindromes over {a, b}
examples.purpose: Mirrored productions: each step adds a matching symbol on both sides.
text: S -> a S a | b S b | a | b | eps

examples.label: Left-recursive expressions
examples.purpose: Operator precedence encoded in the structure of the grammar.

examples.label: Ambiguous arithmetic
examples.purpose: One string with two parse trees, reached by different choices of production.
text: // to see two distinct derivations for the same string
E -> E + E | E * E | ( E ) | id

examples.label: Dangling else
examples.purpose: Classic ambiguity of nested conditionals.
text: S -> if S then S else S | if S then S | a

examples.label: LL(1) arithmetic
examples.purpose: The same expressions as the left-recursive grammar, rewritten for top-down parsing.

examples.label: Equal numbers of a and b
examples.purpose: Context-free, not regular: a and b in any order with equal counts.
text: A -> a | a S | b A A
B -> b | b S | a B B

examples.label: Matched parentheses
examples.purpose: Nested balanced parentheses (the Dyck language).

examples.label: Regular expressions (the regex tool's language)
examples.purpose: Union, concatenation and the postfix operators as three layers of precedence, over a, b, c, d. Quotes write | * + ? ( ) as terminals.

examples.label: Sentences (running example)
examples.purpose: Subject and predicate built from adjective, noun and verb names in angle brackets, such as old Harry snores.

examples.label: Pascal excerpt (declarations)
examples.purpose: A realistic grammar for derivations: choose among productions for declarations, parameters and procedures.
text: <proc> → procedure <phead_c> forward ; | procedure <phead_c> <block> ; | function <fhead_c> forward ; | function <fhead_c> <block> ;

examples.label: aⁿbⁿcⁿ  (n ≥ 1)
examples.purpose: Standard context-sensitive language; not context-free.
text: // LHS sequences use uppercase convention for non-terminals
// Step 1: build a string of n copies of [BC] using S
// Step 2: sort BC pairs left-to-right using CB -> BC
// Step 3: replace leading aB with ab, then cascade b/c
S -> a B c | a S B c

examples.label: aⁿbⁿcⁿdⁿ  (n ≥ 1)
examples.purpose: Four-way counting: the aⁿbⁿcⁿ technique with one more symbol.
text: // Uses marker nonterminals B, C, D that bubble right into place
S -> a B c D | a S B c D

examples.label: Equal a's and b's  (aⁿbⁿ, n ≥ 1)
examples.purpose: A context-free language written with context-sensitive productions, for comparison.
text: // (also context-free, shown here with CSG rules for comparison)
S -> a S b | a b

examples.label: Copy language  (ww)
examples.purpose: Unrestricted productions copy a word; ww is not context-free.
text: // Uses marker X to split and align two copies
X -> X a A | X b B | eps

examples.label: Shrinking rule demo
examples.purpose: A production that shortens the string makes the grammar Type 0.
text: // Generates { aⁿ | n ≥ 0 } with an erasable marker
